subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: A student summarizes the major paired developments of the second week using the mnemonic “week of 2s.” Which summary is complete?

options.text: The trophoblast and embryoblast each form two layers, but the extraembryonic mesoderm remains unsplit and no new cavities form.
The trophoblast forms epiblast and hypoblast, while the embryoblast forms cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.

The trophoblast forms cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast; the embryoblast forms epiblast and hypoblast; extraembryonic mesoderm divides into somatic and splanchnic layers; and two new cavities form.
The trophoblast forms two layers and two cavities, while the embryoblast and extraembryonic mesoderm each remain single-layered.

acceptedFreeText: The trophoblast forms cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast; the embryoblast forms epiblast and hypoblast; extraembryonic mesoderm divides into somatic and splanchnic layers; and two new cavities form.
explanation: The “week of 2s” refers to paired differentiation of the trophoblast, embryoblast, and extraembryonic mesoderm, together with formation of two new cavities: the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac/chorionic cavity.

distractorExplanations.A: This omits the division of extraembryonic mesoderm into somatic and splanchnic layers and the formation of new cavities.
distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the derivatives: epiblast and hypoblast belong to the embryoblast, whereas cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast belong to the trophoblast.
distractorExplanations.C: This correctly includes all of the paired changes summarized by the mnemonic.
distractorExplanations.D: The embryoblast and extraembryonic mesoderm both divide into two layers rather than remaining single-layered.

learningObjective: Recall the paired developmental events represented by the second-week “week of 2s” mnemonic.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is the classic mnemonic for the second week of development, and what does it refer to? Source answer: The 'week of 2s': trophoblast becomes 2 layers (cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast); embryoblast becomes 2 layers (epiblast and hypoblast); extraembryonic mesoderm splits into 2 layers (somatic and splanchnic); and 2 new cavities form (amniotic cavity and yolk sac/chorionic cavity).

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: An approximately day-8 conceptus is examined during implantation. Which description best identifies its position relative to the endometrium?

options.text: It is partially embedded in the endometrial stroma, with implantation still underway.
It is completely embedded in the endometrial stroma, with implantation already complete.
It has not entered the endometrial stroma, so implantation has not begun.
It is partially embedded in the endometrial stroma, but implantation is already complete.

acceptedFreeText: It is partially embedded in the endometrial stroma, with implantation still underway.
explanation: At about day 8, the blastocyst is partially embedded in the endometrial stroma. Implantation has begun but is not yet complete.

distractorExplanations.A: This accurately describes the blastocyst’s location and implantation status at about day 8.
distractorExplanations.B: Complete embedding and completed implantation do not match the partially embedded day-8 blastocyst.
distractorExplanations.C: Implantation is already underway because the blastocyst is partially embedded in the stroma.
distractorExplanations.D: Partial embedding indicates that implantation is still underway, not complete.

learningObjective: Identify the degree of blastocyst implantation at approximately day 8.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: At about day 8, where is the blastocyst located relative to the endometrium? Source answer: At day 8, the blastocyst is partially embedded in the endometrial stroma; implantation is underway but not yet complete.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: Microscopy at day 8 shows an inner trophoblastic layer with distinct mononucleated cells and an outer layer without distinct cell boundaries. Which additional finding correctly completes this identification?

options.text: The inner cytotrophoblast lacks visible mitotic figures, whereas the outer syncytiotrophoblast contains them.
The inner syncytiotrophoblast contains mitotic figures, whereas the outer cytotrophoblast does not.
The inner cytotrophoblast is multinucleated, whereas the outer syncytiotrophoblast is mononucleated.
The inner cytotrophoblast contains mitotic figures, whereas the outer multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast lacks visible mitotic figures.

acceptedFreeText: The inner cytotrophoblast contains mitotic figures, whereas the outer multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast lacks visible mitotic figures.
explanation: The cytotrophoblast is the inner layer of distinct mononucleated cells in which mitoses are seen. The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer without distinct cell boundaries or visible mitotic figures.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the distribution of mitotic figures; they are seen in the cytotrophoblast.
distractorExplanations.B: This reverses both the positions and identities of the trophoblastic layers.
distractorExplanations.C: The cytotrophoblast is mononucleated, while the syncytiotrophoblast is multinucleated.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly matches the structure and mitotic activity of both trophoblastic layers.

learningObjective: Differentiate cytotrophoblast from syncytiotrophoblast by position, cellular structure, and mitotic activity.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: At day 8, what two layers does the trophoblast differentiate into, and how do they differ structurally? Source answer: (1) Cytotrophoblast: inner layer of distinct mononucleated cells where mitoses are seen. (2) Syncytiotrophoblast: outer multinucleated syncytial layer with no distinct cell boundaries and no visible mitotic figures.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: A newly produced trophoblastic cell is destined to contribute a nucleus to the syncytiotrophoblast. Which sequence correctly describes this process?

options.text: It divides within the syncytiotrophoblast, migrates inward, and acquires a distinct cell membrane.
It divides within the cytotrophoblast, migrates outward, and fuses with the syncytiotrophoblast while losing its individual cell membrane.
It divides within the cytotrophoblast, migrates inward, and remains a separate mononucleated cell.
It loses its membrane within the cytotrophoblast before dividing and then remains in the inner layer.

acceptedFreeText: It divides within the cytotrophoblast, migrates outward, and fuses with the syncytiotrophoblast while losing its individual cell membrane.
explanation: Mitotic division occurs in the cytotrophoblast. Cytotrophoblastic cells then migrate outward and fuse with the syncytiotrophoblast, losing their individual cell membranes and adding nuclei to the syncytial layer.

distractorExplanations.A: Mitoses occur in the cytotrophoblast, and contributing cells migrate outward rather than inward.
distractorExplanations.B: This is the correct sequence of division, outward migration, fusion, and membrane loss.
distractorExplanations.C: A cell contributing to the syncytiotrophoblast migrates outward and fuses rather than migrating inward and remaining separate.
distractorExplanations.D: Cytotrophoblastic cells divide before migrating outward and losing their individual membranes during fusion.

learningObjective: Explain how cytotrophoblastic proliferation supplies new nuclei to the syncytiotrophoblast.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Where do mitotic figures occur in the trophoblast, and how do new syncytiotrophoblast nuclei arise? Source answer: Mitoses occur in the cytotrophoblast. Cytotrophoblastic cells divide, migrate outward, and fuse into the syncytiotrophoblast, losing their individual cell membranes.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: A day-8 embryoblast is viewed between the developing cavities. Which arrangement correctly identifies its two cell layers?

options.text: Small cuboidal epiblast cells lie next to the blastocyst cavity, and tall columnar hypoblast cells lie next to the amniotic cavity.
Tall columnar hypoblast cells lie next to the blastocyst cavity, and small cuboidal epiblast cells lie next to the amniotic cavity.
Tall columnar epiblast cells lie next to the amniotic cavity, and small cuboidal hypoblast cells lie next to the blastocyst cavity.
Small cuboidal epiblast and hypoblast cells both lie next to the amniotic cavity.

acceptedFreeText: Tall columnar epiblast cells lie next to the amniotic cavity, and small cuboidal hypoblast cells lie next to the blastocyst cavity.
explanation: At day 8, the embryoblast differentiates into tall columnar epiblast cells adjacent to the amniotic cavity and small cuboidal hypoblast, or primitive endoderm, cells adjacent to the blastocyst cavity.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the morphology, identity, and position of the two layers.
distractorExplanations.B: The cell shapes and cavity relationships are assigned to the wrong layers.
distractorExplanations.C: This correctly identifies the morphology and relative position of both embryoblast layers.
distractorExplanations.D: The layers differ in cell shape and lie adjacent to different cavities.

learningObjective: Identify the morphology and cavity relationships of the epiblast and hypoblast at day 8.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: At day 8, what two layers does the inner cell mass (embryoblast) differentiate into, and what is their relative position? Source answer: (1) Epiblast: upper layer of tall columnar cells adjacent to the amniotic cavity. (2) Hypoblast (primitive endoderm): lower layer of small cuboidal cells adjacent to the blastocyst cavity.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: Which description best defines the bilaminar embryonic disc?

options.text: A flat, two-layered embryoblast composed of epiblast and hypoblast between the dorsal amniotic cavity and ventral blastocyst or yolk-sac cavity.
A flat, two-layered embryoblast composed of epiblast and hypoblast between a dorsal blastocyst cavity and ventral amniotic cavity.
A two-layered trophoblast composed of epiblast and hypoblast surrounding both cavities.
A single-layered embryoblast positioned entirely within the amniotic cavity.

acceptedFreeText: A flat, two-layered embryoblast composed of epiblast and hypoblast between the dorsal amniotic cavity and ventral blastocyst or yolk-sac cavity.
explanation: The bilaminar embryonic disc is the flat, two-layered embryoblast formed by the epiblast and hypoblast. It lies between the amniotic cavity dorsally and the blastocyst or yolk-sac cavity ventrally.

distractorExplanations.A: This correctly defines the disc’s composition, form, and position between the two cavities.
distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the dorsal and ventral cavities.
distractorExplanations.C: The bilaminar disc is an embryoblast structure, not a trophoblast structure.
distractorExplanations.D: The disc has two layers and lies between the cavities rather than entirely within the amniotic cavity.

learningObjective: Define the bilaminar embryonic disc by its layers and spatial relationships.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is the bilaminar embryonic disc, and which layers compose it? Source answer: It is the two-layered embryoblast formed by the epiblast and hypoblast arranged as a flat disc between the amniotic cavity (dorsal) and the blastocyst/yolk sac cavity (ventral).

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: When orienting the bilaminar embryonic disc relative to its adjacent cavities, which relationship is correct?

options.text: Epiblast is ventral toward the amniotic cavity, and hypoblast is dorsal toward the yolk-sac cavity.
Epiblast is dorsal toward the yolk-sac cavity, and hypoblast is ventral toward the amniotic cavity.
Both epiblast and hypoblast are dorsal toward the amniotic cavity.
Epiblast is dorsal toward the amniotic cavity, and hypoblast is ventral toward the blastocyst or yolk-sac cavity.

acceptedFreeText: Epiblast is dorsal toward the amniotic cavity, and hypoblast is ventral toward the blastocyst or yolk-sac cavity.
explanation: The epiblast occupies the dorsal side of the disc toward the amniotic cavity. The hypoblast occupies the ventral side toward the blastocyst or yolk-sac cavity.

distractorExplanations.A: This incorrectly labels the epiblast as ventral and the hypoblast as dorsal.
distractorExplanations.B: Although the dorsal and ventral labels are assigned to the correct layers, each layer is paired with the wrong cavity.
distractorExplanations.C: The hypoblast is ventral rather than dorsal.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly states the orientation of both layers relative to the cavities.

learningObjective: Orient the epiblast and hypoblast along the dorsal–ventral axis of the bilaminar disc.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Which embryonic layer is dorsal and which is ventral in the bilaminar embryonic disc? Source answer: Epiblast is dorsal (toward the amniotic cavity); hypoblast is ventral (toward the blastocyst/yolk sac cavity).

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: At approximately day 9, flattened cells form a membrane along the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast at the abembryonic pole. Which membrane and probable cellular origin are correctly paired?

options.text: Exocoelomic membrane derived from hypoblast cells and lining the outer surface of the cytotrophoblast.
Exocoelomic membrane probably derived from hypoblast cells and lining the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast.
Exocoelomic membrane derived from cytotrophoblast cells and lining the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast.
Exocoelomic membrane probably derived from hypoblast cells and lining the inner surface at the embryonic pole.

acceptedFreeText: Exocoelomic membrane probably derived from hypoblast cells and lining the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast.
explanation: The exocoelomic, or Heuser, membrane forms around day 9 from flattened cells probably derived from the hypoblast. It lines the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast at the abembryonic pole.

distractorExplanations.A: The membrane lines the inner, not outer, surface of the cytotrophoblast.
distractorExplanations.B: This correctly identifies the membrane, its probable hypoblastic origin, and its location.
distractorExplanations.C: The flattened cells are probably derived from the hypoblast rather than the cytotrophoblast.
distractorExplanations.D: The specified location is the abembryonic pole, not the embryonic pole.

learningObjective: Identify the origin and location of the exocoelomic membrane around day 9.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: At the abembryonic pole around day 9, what new membrane forms and from which cells does it likely arise? Source answer: The exocoelomic (Heuser) membrane forms from flattened cells probably derived from the hypoblast; it lines the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast at the abembryonic pole.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: Numerous vacuoles appear in the syncytiotrophoblast around day 9. Which subsequent event and developmental designation are expected?

options.text: Large lacunae divide into numerous vacuoles, initiating the bilaminar stage.
The vacuoles remain separate within the syncytiotrophoblast, initiating the lacunar stage.
The vacuoles fuse into large lacunae, establishing the lacunar stage of trophoblast development.
The vacuoles move into the cytotrophoblast and fuse there, establishing the lacunar stage.

acceptedFreeText: The vacuoles fuse into large lacunae, establishing the lacunar stage of trophoblast development.
explanation: Around day 9, numerous vacuoles within the syncytiotrophoblast fuse to form large lacunae. This change defines the lacunar stage of trophoblast development.

distractorExplanations.A: The sequence is reversed: vacuoles fuse to produce lacunae, and the phase is called the lacunar stage.
distractorExplanations.B: Formation of the large lacunae requires fusion of the vacuoles.
distractorExplanations.C: This correctly describes both the morphologic change and its developmental designation.
distractorExplanations.D: The vacuoles and resulting lacunae are located within the syncytiotrophoblast, not the cytotrophoblast.

learningObjective: Recognize the cellular event defining the lacunar stage of trophoblast development.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: At around day 9, what key change occurs within the syncytiotrophoblast, and what is this phase called? Source answer: Numerous vacuoles appear within the syncytiotrophoblast and fuse to form large lacunae; this is the 'lacunar stage' of trophoblast development.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: New mesodermal tissue appears outside the exocoelomic cavity during the second week. Which description correctly identifies its origin and initial location?

options.text: It arises from cells associated with the yolk sac and first appears between the inner cytotrophoblast and the outer surface of the exocoelomic cavity.
It arises from the cytotrophoblast and first appears inside the exocoelomic cavity.
It arises from the amnion and first appears external to the trophoblast.
It arises from the exocoelomic membrane and first appears between the hypoblast and yolk sac.

acceptedFreeText: It arises from cells associated with the yolk sac and first appears between the inner cytotrophoblast and the outer surface of the exocoelomic cavity.
explanation: Extraembryonic mesoderm arises from cells associated with the yolk sac, including the hypoblast or primary yolk sac. It first appears between the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast and the outer surface of the exocoelomic cavity, filling the space between the trophoblast externally and the amnion or exocoelomic membrane internally.

distractorExplanations.A: This correctly identifies both the yolk-sac-associated origin and the first location of extraembryonic mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.B: Its stated origin is associated with the yolk sac, and it appears outside rather than inside the exocoelomic cavity.
distractorExplanations.C: The described origin is associated with the yolk sac rather than the amnion, and the tissue lies internal to the trophoblast.
distractorExplanations.D: The origin and location do not match the yolk-sac-associated cells and the space between cytotrophoblast and exocoelomic cavity.

learningObjective: Describe the origin and initial position of the extraembryonic mesoderm.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is the origin of the extraembryonic mesoderm and where does it first appear? Source answer: It arises from cells associated with the yolk sac (hypoblast/primary yolk sac) and appears between the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast and the outer surface of the exocoelomic cavity, filling spaces between trophoblast externally and amnion/exocoelomic membrane internally.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: Which sequence correctly explains formation of the extraembryonic, or chorionic, cavity?

options.text: A single space in the extraembryonic mesoderm fragments into many isolated cavities surrounding the primitive yolk sac.
Cavities arise within the amniotic cavity and coalesce into a space surrounding the trophoblast.
Cavities in the extraembryonic mesoderm coalesce into a space that surrounds the primitive yolk sac, amniotic cavity, and the site where the germ disc remains attached.
Large cavities develop in the extraembryonic mesoderm and coalesce into one space surrounding the primitive yolk sac and amniotic cavity, except where the germ disc remains attached.

acceptedFreeText: Large cavities develop in the extraembryonic mesoderm and coalesce into one space surrounding the primitive yolk sac and amniotic cavity, except where the germ disc remains attached.
explanation: Large cavities arise within the extraembryonic mesoderm and then coalesce into a single large extraembryonic, or chorionic, cavity. It surrounds the primitive yolk sac and amniotic cavity except at the attachment of the germ disc.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the process: multiple cavities coalesce into a single large space.
distractorExplanations.B: The cavities develop in the extraembryonic mesoderm, not within the amniotic cavity.
distractorExplanations.C: The new cavity does not occupy the location where the germ disc remains attached.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly states the tissue of origin, coalescence process, resulting space, and exception at the disc attachment.

learningObjective: Explain the sequence by which spaces in extraembryonic mesoderm form the chorionic cavity.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: How does the extraembryonic cavity (chorionic cavity) form? Source answer: Large cavities develop within the extraembryonic mesoderm; these cavities coalesce to form a single large space surrounding the primitive yolk sac and amniotic cavity (except where the germ disc is attached), called the extraembryonic cavity or chorionic cavity.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: After expansion of the chorionic cavity, which description correctly states what it surrounds and how these structures remain connected to the trophoblast?

options.text: It surrounds only the yolk sac, which remains attached by the amniotic cavity.
It surrounds the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac with the embryonic disc; these remain attached to the trophoblast by the connecting stalk.
It surrounds the trophoblast, which remains attached to the embryonic disc by the yolk sac.
It surrounds only the amniotic cavity, which remains attached to the trophoblast by the embryonic disc.

acceptedFreeText: It surrounds the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac with the embryonic disc; these remain attached to the trophoblast by the connecting stalk.
explanation: The chorionic cavity surrounds the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac with the embryonic disc. Their remaining attachment to the trophoblast is a thick cord of extraembryonic mesoderm called the connecting stalk.

distractorExplanations.A: The chorionic cavity surrounds both the amniotic cavity and yolk-sac/embryonic-disc complex, and the attachment is the connecting stalk.
distractorExplanations.B: This correctly identifies the surrounded structures and their connection to the trophoblast.
distractorExplanations.C: The chorionic cavity surrounds the internal amniotic and yolk-sac structures rather than the trophoblast.
distractorExplanations.D: The yolk sac and embryonic disc are also surrounded, and the attachment is the connecting stalk.

learningObjective: Identify the contents surrounded by the chorionic cavity and the role of the connecting stalk.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: Which structures does the extraembryonic cavity (chorionic cavity) surround, and what structure remains as their connection to the trophoblast? Source answer: It surrounds the amniotic cavity and yolk sac/embryonic disc, leaving them attached to the trophoblast only by a thick cord of extraembryonic mesoderm called the connecting stalk.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: At approximately day 13, finger-like projections are observed at the embryonic pole. Which structural description identifies them as primary villi?

options.text: A syncytiotrophoblastic core covered by cytotrophoblast at the abembryonic pole.
A cytotrophoblastic core covered by syncytium at the abembryonic pole.
A cytotrophoblastic core penetrating the syncytiotrophoblast and covered by syncytium at the embryonic pole.
A cytotrophoblastic core covered by syncytium that appears before day 13 at the embryonic pole.

acceptedFreeText: A cytotrophoblastic core penetrating the syncytiotrophoblast and covered by syncytium at the embryonic pole.
explanation: Primary villi appear around day 13 at the embryonic pole. They are finger-like projections with a core of cytotrophoblastic cells that penetrates the syncytiotrophoblast and remains covered by syncytium.

distractorExplanations.A: The core and covering are reversed, and the stated pole is incorrect.
distractorExplanations.B: The structural layers are correct, but primary villi first appear at the embryonic pole rather than the abembryonic pole.
distractorExplanations.C: This correctly identifies the structure, covering, timing, and location of primary villi.
distractorExplanations.D: Primary villi are described as appearing around day 13, not before day 13.

learningObjective: Recognize primary villi by their composition, location, and approximate time of appearance.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are primary villi, and when do they first appear? Source answer: Primary villi are finger-like projections consisting of a core of cytotrophoblastic cells that penetrate into the syncytiotrophoblast and are covered by syncytium; they appear around day 13 at the embryonic pole.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: Which description most accurately defines trophoblastic lacunae and their later connection?

options.text: They are fluid-filled spaces in the syncytiotrophoblast formed by fused vacuoles that later connect with maternal capillaries.
They are fluid-filled spaces in the cytotrophoblast formed by fused vacuoles that later connect with maternal capillaries.
They are spaces in the syncytiotrophoblast formed directly by fusion of maternal capillaries.
They are separate vacuoles in the syncytiotrophoblast that neither fuse nor connect with maternal capillaries.

acceptedFreeText: They are fluid-filled spaces in the syncytiotrophoblast formed by fused vacuoles that later connect with maternal capillaries.
explanation: Trophoblastic lacunae are fluid-filled spaces within the syncytiotrophoblast produced by fusion of vacuoles. They later connect with maternal capillaries and become part of the uteroplacental circulation.

distractorExplanations.A: This correctly describes their location, formation, and later connection with maternal capillaries.
distractorExplanations.B: Trophoblastic lacunae are located in the syncytiotrophoblast rather than the cytotrophoblast.
distractorExplanations.C: They form by fusion of vacuoles; connection with maternal capillaries occurs later.
distractorExplanations.D: The vacuoles fuse into lacunae, which later connect with maternal capillaries.

learningObjective: Define trophoblastic lacunae and describe their formation and later connection.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are trophoblastic lacunae? Source answer: They are fluid-filled spaces within the syncytiotrophoblast that form by fusion of vacuoles; they later connect with maternal capillaries to become part of the uteroplacental circulation.

subject: embryology
topic: Second week: bilaminar disc and implantation
prompt: A learner is reviewing the classic interval encompassing bilaminar-disc development and full implantation in humans. Which timing is most appropriate?

options.text: Entirely before day 8 after fertilization.
Entirely after day 13 after fertilization.
Only on days 8 and 13 after fertilization.
Roughly days 8–13 after fertilization.

explanation: Classic second-week events involving the bilaminar disc and full implantation occur roughly during days 8–13 after fertilization.

distractorExplanations.A: The relevant interval begins at approximately day 8 rather than occurring entirely before it.
distractorExplanations.B: The relevant interval extends through approximately day 13 rather than beginning afterward.
distractorExplanations.C: The interval spans roughly days 8–13; it is not limited to its two boundary days.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly identifies the approximate developmental interval.

learningObjective: Recall the approximate developmental interval associated with the bilaminar disc and full implantation.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: During which approximate days of development does the classic 'second week' embryology (bilaminar disc and full implantation) occur in humans? Source answer: Roughly days 8–13 after fertilization (spanning the second week of development).

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: Which process transforms the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar disc containing ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm during the third week?

options.text: Axial patterning
Gastrulation
Formation of the allantois
Extension of the notochordal process

explanation: Gastrulation is the hallmark process of the third week. It transforms the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc by establishing ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

distractorExplanations.A: Axial patterning specifies body organization but is not the named transformation of the bilaminar disc into three germ layers.
distractorExplanations.B: Gastrulation is correct because it produces the trilaminar disc containing ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.
distractorExplanations.C: The allantois is an endodermal diverticulum and does not describe formation of the trilaminar disc.
distractorExplanations.D: The notochordal process is a mesodermal tube extending from the primitive node, not the overall process that establishes all three germ layers.

learningObjective: Identify gastrulation as the defining process that establishes the trilaminar embryonic disc during the third week.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is the hallmark process of the 3rd week of human development? Source answer: Gastrulation – the transformation of the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc by forming ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: At the beginning of gastrulation, which structure and location should be identified in the embryonic disc?

options.text: The oropharyngeal membrane at the cranial end of the embryonic disc
The cloacal membrane at the caudal end of the embryonic disc
The prechordal plate just caudal to the oropharyngeal membrane
The primitive streak on the dorsal epiblast near the caudal end of the embryonic disc

acceptedFreeText: The primitive streak on the dorsal epiblast near the caudal end of the embryonic disc
explanation: The beginning of gastrulation is marked by formation of the primitive streak on the dorsal surface of the epiblast near the caudal end of the embryonic disc.

distractorExplanations.A: The oropharyngeal membrane marks the future mouth, not the beginning of gastrulation.
distractorExplanations.B: The cloacal membrane marks the future anus and urogenital openings, not the beginning of gastrulation.
distractorExplanations.C: The prechordal plate is a midline mesendodermal thickening formed by early cells migrating through the primitive node; it is not the structure that marks the beginning of gastrulation.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly identifies both the primitive streak and its initial position on the dorsal epiblast near the caudal end.

learningObjective: Identify the primitive streak and its location as the morphological marker of the beginning of gastrulation.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What structure marks the beginning of gastrulation in the human embryo? Source answer: The primitive streak forming on the dorsal surface of the epiblast near the caudal end of the embryonic disc.

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: Which description correctly organizes the primitive streak region along its cranial-caudal extent?

options.text: Cranially, the primitive node with its primitive pit; caudally, the primitive streak with its primitive groove
Cranially, the primitive streak with its primitive groove; caudally, the primitive node with its primitive pit
Cranially, the primitive node with its primitive groove; caudally, the primitive streak with its primitive pit
Cranially, the primitive pit with the cloacal membrane; caudally, the primitive groove with the oropharyngeal membrane

acceptedFreeText: Cranially, the primitive node with its primitive pit; caudally, the primitive streak with its primitive groove
explanation: The cranial end contains the primitive node and its primitive pit. Caudally, the primitive streak contains the primitive groove.

distractorExplanations.A: This is the correct cranial-caudal arrangement of the node, pit, streak, and groove.
distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the cranial and caudal organization: the node and pit are cranial, whereas the streak and groove extend caudally.
distractorExplanations.C: This incorrectly pairs the primitive groove with the node and the primitive pit with the caudal streak.
distractorExplanations.D: The oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes mark future openings and are not paired components of the primitive streak in this manner.

learningObjective: Distinguish the cranial and caudal components of the primitive streak region.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are the key parts of the primitive streak along its cranial-caudal extent? Source answer: Cranially the primitive node with its primitive pit; caudally the primitive streak with the primitive groove.

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: Epiblast cells are observed ingressing through a small depression in the primitive node that is continuous with the primitive groove. Which structure is this?

options.text: Primitive groove
Notochordal process
Primitive pit
Prechordal plate

explanation: The primitive pit is a small depression within the primitive node. It is continuous with the primitive groove and serves as a site of epiblast cell ingression.

distractorExplanations.A: The primitive groove is associated with the caudal primitive streak; the depression specifically located in the primitive node is the primitive pit.
distractorExplanations.B: The notochordal process is a hollow, thick-walled mesodermal tube extending cranially from the primitive node.
distractorExplanations.C: The primitive pit is correctly identified by its position in the primitive node, continuity with the primitive groove, and role in cell ingression.
distractorExplanations.D: The prechordal plate is a midline mesendodermal thickening just caudal to the oropharyngeal membrane.

learningObjective: Identify the primitive pit by its structure, location, and role in epiblast cell ingression.

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: Lineage tracing is performed on the two layers of the bilaminar embryonic disc. Cells from which original layer will contribute to ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm?

Epiblast
Prechordal plate
Notochordal process

explanation: The epiblast is the original bilaminar-disc layer that gives rise to all three embryonic germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm.

distractorExplanations.A: Definitive endoderm is one of the three germ-layer derivatives of the epiblast, not the original layer that produces all three.
distractorExplanations.B: The epiblast is correct because its cells form ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm.
distractorExplanations.C: The prechordal plate is a midline mesendodermal thickening formed by early cells migrating through the primitive node, not the progenitor of all three germ layers.
distractorExplanations.D: The notochordal process is a mesodermal structure arising from prenotochordal cells, not the original source of all three germ layers.

learningObjective: Recognize the epiblast as the progenitor of all three embryonic germ layers.

topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: Which sequence correctly describes formation of intraembryonic mesoderm during gastrulation?

options.text: Epiblast cells pass through the primitive streak and migrate between definitive endoderm and the remaining epiblast
Epiblast cells avoid the primitive streak and remain within the surface ectoderm
Early epiblast cells pass through the primitive node and form a thickening just caudal to the oropharyngeal membrane
Prenotochordal cells pass through the primitive node and form a hollow tube extending cranially

acceptedFreeText: Epiblast cells pass through the primitive streak and migrate between definitive endoderm and the remaining epiblast
explanation: Intraembryonic mesoderm forms when epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak and then migrate into the space between the newly formed definitive endoderm and the remaining epiblast.

distractorExplanations.A: This correctly states both the route through the primitive streak and the final position of intraembryonic mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.B: Epiblast that does not ingress becomes surface ectoderm rather than intraembryonic mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.C: This describes formation of the prechordal plate by some of the earliest cells migrating through the primitive node.
distractorExplanations.D: This describes formation of the notochordal process from prenotochordal cells rather than formation of general intraembryonic mesoderm.

learningObjective: Describe the cellular movements and final position involved in intraembryonic mesoderm formation.

source.excerpt: Source prompt: How is intraembryonic mesoderm formed during gastrulation? Source answer: Epiblast cells pass through the primitive streak and then migrate between the newly formed definitive endoderm and the remaining epiblast to form intraembryonic mesoderm.

topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning

distractorExplanations.C: The prechordal plate forms from some of the earliest cells that migrate through the primitive node and move cranially.

prompt: A hollow, thick-walled tube of mesoderm extends cranially from the primitive node. Which structure is it, and from which cells does it arise?

Primitive pit, from epiblast cells remaining on the surface
Notochordal process, from prenotochordal cells migrating through the primitive node
Allantois, from endoderm of the posterior yolk-sac wall

distractorExplanations.C: This correctly pairs the notochordal process with its structure, direction of extension, and prenotochordal-cell origin.
distractorExplanations.D: The allantois is an endodermal diverticulum extending from the posterior yolk-sac wall into the connecting stalk, not a tube extending from the primitive node.

learningObjective: Identify the notochordal process and its origin from prenotochordal cells migrating through the primitive node.

explanation: The prechordal plate is a midline mesendodermal thickening located just caudal to the oropharyngeal membrane. It is formed by some of the earliest cells to migrate through the primitive node and move cranially.

distractorExplanations.B: The notochordal process is a hollow mesodermal tube arising from prenotochordal cells; non-ingressing epiblast becomes surface ectoderm.

prompt: An embryologist describes the three mutually orthogonal dimensions that specify overall body organization. Which set names these body axes correctly?

options.text: Cranial-caudal, medial-lateral, and proximal-distal
Dorsal-ventral, superficial-deep, and left-right
Cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, and proximal-distal

explanation: The three body axes are cranial-caudal, also called anterior-posterior; dorsal-ventral, corresponding to back-belly; and left-right.

distractorExplanations.C: This substitutes proximal-distal for the left-right axis.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly lists all three orthogonal body axes: cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, and left-right.

learningObjective: Name the three orthogonal axes that organize the embryonic body plan.

source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is meant by ‘body axes’ in embryology? Source answer: The three orthogonal axes specifying body organization: cranial-caudal (anterior-posterior), dorsal-ventral (back-belly), and left-right.

A change limited to formation of the surface ectoderm
A change limited to formation of the allantois

distractorExplanations.C: The expected consequence concerns laterality and organ position, not an isolated change in surface ectoderm formation.

Persistent allantoic remnants
Persistent primitive streak remnants
Persistent notochordal-process remnants

distractorExplanations.D: The notochordal process is a mesodermal tube arising from prenotochordal cells and is not the remnant identified as the frequent origin of this tumor.

learningObjective: Relate sacrococcygeal teratoma containing all three germ layers to persistent primitive streak remnants.

subject: embryology
topic: Fourth week: body folding
prompt: Which pair of processes best characterizes the fourth week of embryonic development?

options.text: Persistence of an undifferentiated trilaminar disc and proportional enlargement of the yolk sac
Differentiation of the germ layers into organ primordia and body folding into a tube-within-a-tube plan
Formation of a tubular body without differentiation of the trilaminar germ layers
Differentiation of the germ layers while the embryonic disc remains flat

acceptedFreeText: Differentiation of the germ layers into organ primordia and body folding into a tube-within-a-tube plan
explanation: The fourth week is characterized by differentiation of the trilaminar germ layers into the primordia of most major organ systems and folding of the embryonic disc to establish a tube-within-a-tube body plan.

distractorExplanations.A: The fourth week involves differentiation and body folding, not persistence of an undifferentiated flat disc.
distractorExplanations.B: This correctly combines the two defining processes: germ-layer differentiation and establishment of the tube-within-a-tube body plan.
distractorExplanations.C: Body folding is accompanied by differentiation of the trilaminar germ layers into organ primordia.
distractorExplanations.D: The embryonic disc does not remain flat; body folding converts it into a three-dimensional tubular form.

learningObjective: Identify the two principal developmental processes that characterize the fourth week.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What are the two key processes that characterize the 4th week of embryonic development? Source answer: 1) Differentiation of trilaminar germ layers into primordia of most major organ systems 2) Body folding of the embryonic disc to establish the tube-within-a-tube body plan

subject: embryology
topic: Fourth week: body folding
prompt: During the fourth week, the embryonic disc bulges and folds around the yolk sac. Which process is the principal mechanical driver of this change?

options.text: Fusion of the right and left germ layers at the ventral midline
Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition of neural crest precursors
Wedge-shaped cell activity at dorsolateral hinge points
Rapid growth of the embryonic disc and amnion relative to the minimally growing yolk sac

acceptedFreeText: Rapid growth of the embryonic disc and amnion relative to the minimally growing yolk sac
explanation: Differential growth drives body folding: the embryonic disc and amnion grow rapidly, especially in length, while the yolk sac grows little. The expanding disc consequently bulges and folds around the relatively static yolk sac.

distractorExplanations.A: Ventral midline fusion is an event produced during folding, not the principal mechanical driver described here.
distractorExplanations.B: Neural crest epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition produces migratory cells rather than driving folding of the entire embryonic disc.
distractorExplanations.C: Dorsolateral hinge points help bring neural folds together, particularly in the cranial region; they are not the main driver of overall body folding.
distractorExplanations.D: This is correct because unequal growth of the disc and amnion relative to the yolk sac mechanically produces folding.

learningObjective: Explain how differential growth mechanically produces embryonic body folding.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: What is the main mechanical driver of embryonic body folding in the 4th week? Source answer: Differential growth: the embryonic disc (and amnion) grows rapidly, especially in length, while the yolk sac grows little, causing the disc to bulge and fold around the relatively static yolk sac

Cranial folding around day 22, followed by lateral and caudal folding around day 23
Lateral folding around day 22, followed by cranial and caudal folding around day 23

subject: embryology
topic: Fourth week: body folding
prompt: Which coordinated movement transforms the initially flat embryonic disc into a three-dimensional tubular body form?

options.text: The disc edges move dorsally and laterally and remain separate
The disc edges move ventrally and laterally and fuse at the dorsal midline
The cranial, lateral, and caudal edges move ventrally and medially and fuse at the ventral midline
The cranial and caudal edges move medially while the lateral edges remain fixed

acceptedFreeText: The cranial, lateral, and caudal edges move ventrally and medially and fuse at the ventral midline
explanation: During body folding, the cranial, lateral, and caudal edges are brought ventrally and medially toward one another. Their fusion along the ventral midline converts the flat disc into a three-dimensional tubular body.

distractorExplanations.A: The edges move ventrally and medially rather than dorsally and laterally, and they ultimately fuse.
distractorExplanations.B: Although the movement is ventral, it is also medial, and fusion occurs along the ventral rather than dorsal midline.
distractorExplanations.C: This correctly describes the direction of movement, the site of fusion, and the resulting tubular body form.
distractorExplanations.D: All three regional edges participate; the lateral edges do not remain fixed.

learningObjective: Describe the direction and outcome of embryonic disc-edge movement during body folding.

source.excerpt: Source prompt: What happens to the cranial, lateral, and caudal edges of the embryonic disc during folding? Source answer: They are brought ventrally and medially toward each other and fuse along the ventral midline, converting the flat disc into a 3-D tubular body form

subject: embryology
topic: Fourth week: body folding
prompt: Which mechanism converts the initially flat embryonic endoderm into the primitive gut tube during the fourth week?

options.text: Cranial folding alone rolls the endoderm into a single undivided tube
Cranial, caudal, and lateral folding approximate and fuse endodermal edges to form the foregut, midgut, and hindgut
Lateral folding separates the endoderm into right and left tubes that remain unfused
Caudal folding moves the endoderm dorsally while its edges remain apart

acceptedFreeText: Cranial, caudal, and lateral folding approximate and fuse endodermal edges to form the foregut, midgut, and hindgut
explanation: Cranial, caudal, and lateral folding bring the endodermal edges together and cause them to fuse. This converts the flat endodermal layer into the tubular foregut, midgut, and hindgut.

distractorExplanations.A: Gut-tube formation requires cranial, caudal, and lateral folding rather than cranial folding alone.
distractorExplanations.B: This correctly identifies both the folding mechanism and formation of the foregut, midgut, and hindgut.
distractorExplanations.C: The endodermal edges come together and fuse; they do not remain as separate right and left tubes.
distractorExplanations.D: The endodermal edges are approximated and fused rather than remaining apart.

learningObjective: Explain how multidirectional body folding creates the primitive gut tube.

source.title: Course-aligned embryology study notes
source.excerpt: Source prompt: How does the flat embryonic endoderm become the gut tube during the 4th week? Source answer: Cranial, caudal, and lateral folding bring endodermal edges together and fuse them, converting the flat endoderm into a tubular structure: foregut, midgut, and hindgut

subject: embryology
topic: Fourth week: body folding
prompt: Which statement correctly describes the progressive separation of the midgut from the yolk sac?

options.text: Cranial folding immediately disconnects the midgut from the yolk sac during week 4
Caudal folding broadens the yolk-sac neck until the midgut becomes tubular at the end of week 6
Lateral folding completely disconnects the midgut from the yolk sac by the end of week 6
Lateral folding progressively narrows the yolk-sac neck, leaving a narrow vitelline duct connection at the end of week 6

distractorExplanations.B: The yolk-sac neck is narrowed by lateral folding rather than broadened by caudal folding.
distractorExplanations.C: A narrow vitelline duct still connects the fully tubular midgut to the yolk sac at the end of week 6.
distractorExplanations.D: This correctly states the mechanism, timing, and remaining connection.

learningObjective: Relate progressive lateral folding to narrowing of the yolk-sac connection and formation of the tubular midgut.

It remains at the unfolded caudal edge of the embryonic disc
